name: She's a Super Leek Burger - (Comes with braised leeks)

recipe.history:
The leek (Allium ampeloprasum var. porrum) is one of the oldest cultivated vegetables in the world, tracing its roots back more than four thousand years to ancient Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean. Hieroglyphics carved into the walls of the pyramids at Giza reference leeks as a staple food of the laborers who built them, and ancient Roman texts — including those of Pliny the Elder — record that Emperor Nero consumed leeks daily, believing they strengthened his singing voice. Unlike their sharper cousins the onion and garlic, leeks carry a gentle, almost aristocratic sweetness, a quality that made them beloved throughout medieval Europe. Wales adopted the leek as its national symbol, a distinction that endures to this day and is celebrated every St. David's Day on the first of March, when Welsh men and women proudly wear leeks pinned to their lapels. French cuisine elevated the leek to near-sacred status — it is the quiet backbone of vichyssoise, pot-au-feu, and the classic bouquet garni, earning it the tender nickname "the asparagus of the poor" among peasant cooks who understood that something humble, prepared with patience, could become something transcendent.

For most of American culinary history, the leek was an afterthought — a garnish, a soup vegetable, something your grandmother might grow in her kitchen garden but that never truly broke through into the mainstream. The hamburger, that most American of inventions, was for decades a study in bold, uncomplicated flavors: beef, mustard, ketchup, pickles, maybe a slice of American cheese. But as the farm-to-table movement gathered momentum in the late 1990s and accelerated through the 2000s, American chefs began raiding their grandmothers' gardens and their European cookbooks with fresh eyes. Braised and caramelized alliums — onions, shallots, ramps, and eventually leeks — became the topping of choice for chefs who wanted to add sweetness and depth to the burger without overwhelming the beef. The braise, in particular, transforms the leek entirely: the fibrous, sometimes sharp raw vegetable becomes silky, yielding, and almost buttery, with a concentrated sweetness that plays against the charred crust of a well-seared patty in a way that feels both unexpected and inevitable. Gastropubs and better burger joints across the country began featuring braised leeks as a premium topping, and the ingredient slowly found its deserved place in the American burger canon.

I remember the first time I truly understood what a leek could do to a burger. It was a grey November afternoon, the kind where the sky sits low and the cold gets into your coat no matter how many layers you're wearing, and I had ducked into a small restaurant on a side street I'd never noticed before. The place smelled of brown butter and thyme. I ordered the special — a burger with braised leeks — mostly because I was cold and it was the first thing my eyes landed on. What arrived was quieter than I expected: no towering architecture, no aggressive sauces jostling for attention. Just a soft, golden bun, a patty with a crust that crackled when I pressed it, and a tangle of leeks that had been cooked down into something almost jammy, pale green and glistening. The first bite stopped me. The leeks were sweet in a way that was almost melancholy, the way late afternoon light is sweet, and the beef underneath was still faintly pink at the center, yielding and rich. I sat there alone at the counter and ate slowly, looking out at the wet street, and felt, briefly, that everything was exactly where it was supposed to be. That burger has lived in me ever since.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a beef burger patty, and it is medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, or 54 to 57 degrees Celsius. This is not a matter of preference — it is a matter of physics, chemistry, and respect for the animal and the cook. At medium rare, the myoglobin in the beef has transformed just enough to render the fat silky and the muscle fibers tender without squeezing out the moisture that gives a patty its soul. Cook a patty beyond this point and you are conducting an act of slow extraction — wringing out the juices, toughening the proteins, turning something alive and complex into something dry and apologetic. The argument against medium rare — food safety — is real but narrowly applicable: it concerns ground beef that has been handled poorly or sourced carelessly. Start with freshly ground, quality beef from a trusted butcher, handle it with cold hands and minimal pressure, and cook it on a screaming-hot surface that sears the exterior immediately, and a medium-rare patty is not only safe but is the fullest expression of what a burger can be. A well-done burger is a burger that has given up. A medium-rare burger is a burger that has arrived.
ingredients: 300g bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
For the burger patties (makes 4 x 6oz patties):
680g (1.5 lbs) freshly ground beef, 80/20 chuck-to-fat ratio
1 tbsp neutral oil (e.g., canola or grapeseed), for cooking
4 large leeks, white and light-green parts only
For the Dijon crème fraîche sauce:
instructions: 1. Make the brioche bun dough: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine the bread flour, instant yeast, sugar, and salt. In a small bowl, whisk together the warm milk and 2 eggs. With the mixer on low, pour in the milk-egg mixture and mix until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes.

2. Increase mixer speed to medium and knead the dough for 5 minutes until it begins to come together. With the mixer running, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to be fully incorporated before adding the next. This will take 8–10 minutes. Once all butter is added, increase to medium-high and knead for a further 6–8 minutes until the dough is smooth, glossy, and passes the windowpane test (a small piece stretched thin should be translucent without tearing).

3. Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature for 1.5–2 hours until doubled in size. Alternatively, refrigerate overnight for a slower, more flavorful rise.

4. Divide the risen dough into 4 equal portions (approximately 130g each). Shape each into a tight, smooth ball by pulling the surface of the dough under itself and pinching the seam. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing them at least 3 inches apart. Cover loosely and proof for 45–60 minutes until puffed and pillowy.

5. Preheat the oven to 375°F / 190°C. Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp of water to make an egg wash. Gently brush the tops of the buns with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown and the internal temperature reads 190°F / 88°C. Transfer to a wire rack to cool completely before slicing.

6. Prepare the leeks: Trim the dark green tops and root ends from the leeks. Slice them in half lengthwise, then cut crosswise into 1.5-inch pieces. Submerge in a large bowl of cold water and agitate vigorously to release any grit. Lift the leeks out of the water (do not pour — let the grit sink), drain, and pat dry with a clean kitchen towel.

7. Braise the leeks: In a wide, heavy-bottomed skillet or sauté pan, melt the butter over medium heat until foaming subsides. Add the sliced garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant but not browned. Add the leeks and season with salt and white pepper. Toss to coat and cook, stirring occasionally, for 5–6 minutes until the leeks begin to soften and turn translucent at the edges.

8. Pour in the white wine and let it simmer for 2 minutes, scraping up any fond from the bottom of the pan. Add the stock, thyme sprigs, and bay leaf. Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and braise for 18–22 minutes, stirring once halfway through, until the leeks are completely tender and silky and most of the liquid has been absorbed or reduced to a light glaze. Remove the thyme sprigs and bay leaf, stir in the lemon juice, and adjust seasoning. Keep warm over the lowest heat setting.

9. Make the Dijon crème fraîche sauce: In a small bowl, whisk together the crème fraîche, both mustards, lemon juice, grated garlic, salt, and pepper until smooth and well combined. Fold in the chives. Taste and adjust seasoning. Refrigerate until needed — the sauce will firm slightly as it chills, which is ideal for spreading.

10. Form the patties: Remove the ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 170g / 6oz each). Working quickly and with minimal handling — overworking the beef will compact the proteins and toughen the patty — gently form each portion into a disc roughly 4 inches in diameter and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Season generously on both sides with flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper immediately before cooking.

11. Cook the patties to medium rare: Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat for at least 3 minutes until it is ripping hot and just beginning to smoke. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat. Working in batches if needed to avoid crowding, place the patties in the pan. Do not press. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep mahogany crust has formed on the underside. Flip once. Cook for a further 2–2.5 minutes. In the final 60 seconds of cooking, lay a slice of Gruyère over each patty and cover the pan loosely with a lid or foil to allow the cheese to melt. Target an internal temperature of 130–135°F / 54–57°C for medium rare — use an instant-read thermometer to verify. Transfer to a wire rack to rest for 3 minutes. Do not skip the rest.

12. Toast the buns: While the patties rest, melt the butter in a clean skillet or on the griddle over medium heat. Place the buns cut-side down and toast for 1.5–2 minutes until golden and lightly crisped. Remove and set aside.

13. Assemble the burgers: Spread a generous tablespoon of the Dijon crème fraîche sauce on the cut face of both the top and bottom bun. Place a small handful of baby arugula on the bottom bun. Set the rested, cheese-draped patty on top of the arugula. Spoon a generous mound of the warm braised leeks over the melted Gruyère, letting them cascade naturally over the sides. Finish with a small pinch of flaky sea salt over the leeks. Cap with the top bun, press gently, and serve immediately.
